projects.sectionIntro: Seven projects taken from concept to production, for clients in tourism, real estate and graphic design. Each solved a concrete problem rather than just changing how a page looks.
projects.p1Desc: Custom web solution for the Sottomonte agency: Building a high-performance responsive system. Advanced SEO optimization and a custom layout designed for maximum conversion and loading speed.
projects.p2Desc: Custom web solution for presenting premium accommodation on the Pelješac peninsula. System designed focusing on visual content loading speed and responsive design ensuring ease of booking on all devices.
projects.p3Desc: Sabioncello: From design concept to a complete destination guide. Development of a modern and scalable web solution optimized for an international audience, with emphasis on visual storytelling and technical SEO excellence.
projects.p4Desc: Sabioncello Grafika: A modern web application for graphic design services, built in React. A scalable design ecosystem emphasizing visual presentation, contemporary UX, and technical excellence.
projects.p5Desc: Dani Cvjetnog: A custom web solution for a student event. Interactive sign-up forms for games and clear event information, designed for easy navigation and a smooth visitor experience.
projects.p4MetaTitle: Sabioncello Grafika: React app for a graphic design studio
projects.p4MetaDesc: A React web application for graphic design studio Sabioncello Grafika: fast, responsive presentation of services and a modern user experience.
projects.p4Intro: Sabioncello Grafika is a graphic design studio that needed a digital presence matching its own visual standard. Rather than a conventional brochure site, the project was built as a React application, fast, modular, and easy to extend with new services.
projects.p4Challenge: A studio whose business is visual identity cannot afford a generic website. Two things that usually pull against each other had to be reconciled: rich visual presentation of the work, and load speed on mobile, where most visits arrive. The service offering also changes, so the structure had to absorb new content without a redesign.
projects.p4Approach: The application was built in React with Vite, using a component structure where each service is a separate, reusable element. Images are optimised and served in modern formats, and the layout was developed mobile-first. Particular attention went to typography and white space, keeping the studio’s work in the foreground and the interface out of the way.
projects.p4F1: Component-based React architecture that absorbs new services without design changes
projects.p4F2: Mobile-first responsive layout tested across a wide range of screen sizes
projects.p4F3: Optimised imagery and minimal JavaScript for fast loading
projects.p4F4: Clean typographic hierarchy that keeps the visual work in focus
projects.p4Delivered: A production application was delivered on its own domain, ready for further content expansion, with a documented code structure for future changes.
projects.p1MetaTitle: Sottomonte: WordPress website for a real estate agency
projects.p1MetaDesc: A WordPress website for real estate agency Sottomonte: a clear property catalogue, technical SEO groundwork and fast page loads.
projects.p1Intro: Sottomonte is a real estate agency that needed a site taking two things seriously: a clear presentation of its listings, and visibility in search. The solution was built on WordPress so the client could maintain listings independently.
projects.p1Challenge: Property listings change constantly, so editing content could not depend on a developer. At the same time, property pages are image-heavy, which easily destroys load speed, and speed together with technical SEO decides whether the listings get found at all.
projects.p1Approach: WordPress was set up with a content structure tailored to properties and templates that hold a consistent layout regardless of who enters the data. On the technical side the SEO groundwork was implemented: a semantic heading hierarchy, meta data, optimised images and a clean URL scheme. The layout was developed responsively, with emphasis on browsing listings on a phone.
projects.p1F1: Independent listing management through WordPress, with no developer in the loop
projects.p1F2: Technical SEO groundwork: semantic headings, meta data and clean URLs
projects.p1F3: Optimised property imagery for fast loading over mobile networks
projects.p1F4: Responsive layout tuned for browsing the catalogue on a phone
projects.p1Delivered: The site went live on its own domain, handed over with documentation for entering and maintaining content.
projects.p2MetaTitle: Visit Eva Orebić: website for tourist accommodation on Pelješac
projects.p2MetaDesc: A WordPress site for Visit Eva accommodation in Orebić: visual presentation, fast-loading galleries and a straightforward booking contact.
projects.p2Intro: Visit Eva Orebić presents private accommodation in Orebić on the Pelješac peninsula. The goal was for a guest to get a clear picture of the property and its surroundings within seconds, and to find the booking contact without hunting for it.
projects.p2Challenge: Tourism content is almost entirely visual, large photo galleries are essential, yet they are also the heaviest load on page speed. On top of that, much of the traffic arrives from mobile devices and from abroad, often on slower networks where every unnecessary second is felt directly.
projects.p2Approach: Photographs were processed and served at optimised sizes, with galleries below the fold loaded lazily. The page structure walks the visitor through linearly: the accommodation, its amenities, the surroundings, then contact. WordPress was configured so the owner can refresh photos and seasonal information without technical knowledge.
projects.p2F1: Optimised galleries with lazy loading below the fold
projects.p2F2: Linear structure that guides the visitor toward the booking contact
projects.p2F3: Seasonal content updates without technical knowledge
projects.p2F4: Responsive presentation suited to guests searching from a phone
projects.p2Delivered: The site was published on its own domain and handed over with instructions for seasonal content maintenance.
projects.p3MetaTitle: Sabioncello: destination web guide for the Pelješac peninsula
projects.p3MetaDesc: A destination web guide for Pelješac: content architecture for an international audience, visual storytelling and technical SEO.
projects.p3Intro: Sabioncello is a destination guide for the Pelješac peninsula, aimed primarily at international visitors. The project started from a design concept and grew into a complete content system.
projects.p3Challenge: A destination guide poses a different problem from a presentation site: there is a lot of content and it has to stay findable. Visitors arrive with different intentions, beaches, wine, accommodation, activities, so the structure has to absorb growth without becoming unnavigable. The audience is international, which places demands on both language and load speed from abroad.
projects.p3Approach: Content was organised into clear thematic sections with consistent templates, so every new page automatically inherits the correct heading structure and internal linking. Technical SEO was treated as part of the architecture rather than a later addition: semantic headings, descriptive URLs and optimised images. The visual language leans on landscape photography with restrained typography.
projects.p3F1: Thematic content architecture that scales with the number of pages
projects.p3F2: Internal linking that carries visitors through related topics
projects.p3F3: Technical SEO built into the templates rather than bolted on
projects.p3F4: Visual storytelling built on destination photography
projects.p3Delivered: The guide was published and structured so new destinations and topics can be added without further development work.
projects.p5MetaTitle: Dani Cvjetnog: website for a student event
projects.p5MetaDesc: A website for the Dani Cvjetnog student event: programme overview, interactive sign-up forms and instant loading with no CMS.
projects.p5Intro: Dani Cvjetnog is a student event that needed a simple site carrying the programme and sign-ups for its games. Given the short-lived purpose and the need for speed, it was built without a CMS, plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
projects.p5Challenge: Event sites have highly concentrated traffic: most visits happen in the few days before the event, largely from mobile devices. The site had to be instantly available with no database dependency, and the sign-ups simple enough to complete on the first attempt.
projects.p5Approach: The site was written as a static set of files, which removed an entire layer of things that can fail in production. Sign-up forms were implemented in JavaScript with client-side validation and clear error messages. The programme is laid out for legibility on a small screen.
projects.p5F1: Static build with no database, a minimal surface for failure
projects.p5F2: Interactive sign-up forms with validation and clear error messages
projects.p5F3: Programme layout readable on a mobile screen
projects.p5F4: Instant loading thanks to the absence of a CMS layer
projects.p5Delivered: The site was published ahead of the event and used throughout the programme.
projects.p6Subtitle: Website for a campsite on Pelješac
projects.p6Desc: Camping Lovište Paradise: a single-page React application for a family-run campsite in Lovište bay. Presentation of the pitches and facilities, a multilingual interface, and a clear path to a booking enquiry.
projects.p6MetaTitle: Camping Lovište Paradise: website for a campsite on Pelješac
projects.p6MetaDesc: A React website for Camping Lovište Paradise: presenting the terraced pitches, the camp facilities and the surrounding area, with a multilingual interface and an enquiry form.
projects.p6Intro: Camping Lovište Paradise is a family-run campsite in Lovište bay on the western tip of the Pelješac peninsula. It needed a site that explains to an international guest, within seconds, what the camp is like, what it offers and how to book, without burying them in detail.
projects.p6Challenge: A campsite is chosen visually, but the decision is made on specifics: what the sanitary block is like, whether there is shade, how far the sea is, whether pets are allowed. A large amount of practical information had to sit alongside a presentation that stays calm and easy to scan. The audience is mostly international and arrives on mobile, usually while still planning the trip.
projects.p6Approach: The site was built as a single-page React application with Vite, split into clear sections: a sense of the location, the camp facilities, the sanitary block, activities in the area, and distances to nearby places. The content is multilingual, and the photography is organised into galleries that load progressively. Every section ends with a clear route to the enquiry form.
projects.p6F1: Single-page React architecture with clearly separated thematic sections
projects.p6F2: Multilingual interface for guests arriving from different countries
projects.p6F3: Photo galleries of the camp, the sanitary block and the surroundings, loaded progressively
projects.p6F4: Distances to nearby destinations and a map, for easier trip planning
projects.p6Delivered: The site was published on its own domain, structured so content and seasonal information can be added without development work.
projects.p7Desc: BMFit: a conversion-focused landing page for personal trainer Benjamin Matošević. It walks the visitor from the problem to a sign-up, with a clear account of the programme and answers to common objections.
projects.p7MetaTitle: BMFit: landing page for a fitness coaching programme
projects.p7MetaDesc: A landing page for the BMFit coaching programme: a structure that carries the visitor from problem to sign-up, loading instantly with no CMS layer.
projects.p7Intro: BMFit is Benjamin Matošević’s personal training programme, aimed at women who have started and stopped several times before. The page has a single job: explain why the previous attempts failed, and turn that recognition into a sign-up.
projects.p7Challenge: A single-goal landing page misses more easily than a full website. The visitor arrives sceptical, often after a bad experience, and leaves within seconds if they do not recognise their own situation. The order of the argument had to be arranged so each section answers the question the previous one raises, without tipping into a hard sell.
projects.p7Approach: The page was built as a static set of files with no CMS, which gives it instant loading and a minimal surface for failure. The content is sequenced as an argument: the problem, the cause, a three-step system, who runs the programme, and answers to common questions, with every section leading back to the same sign-up form. The visual language is a dark ground with a single accent tone, so the calls to action stay unmistakable.
projects.p7F1: Static build with no CMS, loading instantly
projects.p7F2: Content sequenced as an argument, from problem through to sign-up
projects.p7F3: Three-step programme breakdown and a frequently-asked-questions section
projects.p7F4: Consistent calls to action all leading to the same sign-up form
projects.p7Delivered: The page was published on its own domain, with a simple structure that allows the offer to be revised and new messaging tested without development work.

aboutPage.metaTitle: About | Martin Bogoje, software developer in Zagreb
aboutPage.metaDesc: Software developer based in Zagreb: MSc studies at FER, experience at Ericsson Nikola Tesla, and seven client web projects across tourism, real estate and design.
aboutPage.label: About
aboutPage.title: Who I am
aboutPage.lead: Martin Bogoje, a software developer based in Zagreb. I build websites and applications for clients who need the site to work as a tool rather than decoration: fast, clear, and findable.
aboutPage.p1: I am currently completing a master’s degree in computing at the Faculty of Electrical Engineering and Computing, University of Zagreb, specialising in software engineering and information systems, after finishing my undergraduate degree at the same faculty.
aboutPage.p2: I worked as a Software Developer at Ericsson Nikola Tesla, one of the largest technology companies in the region. That taught me what independent projects rarely do: what code looks like when somebody else has to maintain it, why documentation gets written, and how much process sits behind a single release.
aboutPage.p3: Alongside that I started taking on my own clients. So far that is seven projects carried from concept to production: a real estate agency, a campsite, a destination guide, private accommodation, a graphic design studio, a fitness coaching programme and a student event. Most come from tourism and real estate on the Pelješac peninsula and the surrounding area.
aboutPage.p4: I work with React and Vite when a project calls for an application, and with WordPress when the client needs to maintain the content themselves. On the backend, Node.js, C# and PostgreSQL. Technical SEO and load speed are part of the job rather than an add-on service.
aboutPage.p5: I work in Croatian, English and German, and this site also exists in Polish. That is not incidental: a large share of the visitors my clients serve arrive from abroad, so multilingual delivery is more often a requirement than an exception.
aboutPage.how: I start from what the site has to achieve, not from how it should look. Content structure comes next, then design, then build. Before handover I check speed, the mobile view and the technical SEO groundwork. The client gets something they can maintain themselves, plus the documentation to do it.
aboutPage.fact1: MSc in computing at FER, University of Zagreb
aboutPage.fact2: Former Software Developer at Ericsson Nikola Tesla
aboutPage.fact3: Seven client projects in production, from React applications to WordPress sites
aboutPage.fact4: Working in Croatian, English and German
aboutPage.p6: Beyond the build itself, part of the job is getting it live: domain, hosting and certificates, checking the result on real devices, and handing the site over in a state the client can take on without me. Every project I have worked on so far is online and in use today, which is the only test that really counts.

privacyPage.metaDesc: How data is handled on bogojemartin.com: what is collected, why, how long it is kept, and what rights you have under the GDPR.
privacyPage.label: Legal
privacyPage.title: Privacy policy
privacyPage.lead: This site collects as little as possible. No forms, no profiling, and no tracking cookies.
privacyPage.controller: The controller of personal data is Martin Bogoje, Zagreb, Croatia. For any question about data processing, I am reachable at the email address given at the bottom of this page.
privacyPage.data: The site has no contact form and no user accounts, so I do not collect data that you enter yourself. If you email me, I process your address and the content of your message solely in order to answer the enquiry. The legal basis is legitimate interest, or taking steps prior to entering into a contract.
privacyPage.analyticsOn: Visitor numbers are measured with cookieless analytics that stores no identifier on your device and does not follow you across other sites. Data is collected in aggregate, without personal data, and is used only to see how many visits there are and which pages are read.
privacyPage.analyticsOff: There are currently no analytics, tracking or advertising tools on this site. No cookies are placed in your browser, which is also why this site shows no cookie notice.
privacyPage.hosting: The site is static and served through a hosting provider which, like any web server, records technical details about requests, including IP address, browser type and time of access. These logs exist for security and reliability and are not used to identify visitors.
privacyPage.rights: Under the General Data Protection Regulation you have the right to access your data, to rectification, erasure, restriction of processing and to object to processing. If you believe your rights have been infringed, you may lodge a complaint with the Croatian Personal Data Protection Agency or your local supervisory authority.
privacyPage.retention: Email correspondence is kept for as long as it takes to answer the enquiry and handle any resulting work, and is deleted afterwards. Technical server logs are deleted according to the hosting provider’s policy.
privacyPage.contact: For any question about how your data is handled, or a request for access or erasure, send me an email and I will respond within a reasonable period.

services.indexMetaTitle: Services: web development and maintenance | Martin Bogoje
services.indexMetaDesc: Website and application development, sites for tourism and holiday rentals, plus maintenance and technical SEO. Based in Zagreb, Croatia.
services.indexLead: Three things I do, described the way they actually go: what you get, how the process runs, and who each one is for.
services.ctaText: Send a few lines about what you need and I will come back with questions and a proposed approach, with no obligation.
services.s1MetaTitle: Website development in Zagreb | Martin Bogoje
services.s1MetaDesc: Website and web application development in React or WordPress: design, build, technical SEO and going live. Based in Zagreb, Croatia.
services.s1Lead: A site that does the job you commissioned it for: explains the offer, brings in enquiries, and looks as good on a phone as on a large screen.
services.s1Intro1: I build websites from the first conversation through to the moment they are live and in use. That covers content structure, design, the build, testing on real devices, and setting up the domain and hosting. What the client ends up with is something they can maintain themselves, not something that depends on me every time a phone number changes.
services.s1Intro2: There is no single type of site that suits everyone. A small business brochure site, a property catalogue and a single-goal landing page are three different problems and need three different answers. So I start by asking what the site has to achieve, and only then do we pick the technology.
services.s1Intro3: Price and timeline depend on scope, so I do not publish a fixed rate card that would be wrong for half the enquiries anyway. After a short conversation I can tell you whether the project is feasible, roughly how long it takes and what it costs, and you get that before anything is agreed.
services.s1Get1: Design built around your content, not a template that content is later forced into
services.s1Get2: Responsive layout tested on real phones, not only in developer tools
services.s1Get3: Technical SEO groundwork: semantic headings, meta data, clean URLs and optimised images
services.s1Get4: Fast loading, because most visits arrive over mobile networks rather than office wi-fi
services.s1Get5: Going live with domain, hosting and certificate, plus instructions for maintaining it yourself
services.s1Step1: Conversation and scope. We go through what the site has to achieve, who the audience is and what content already exists. That produces a page list and a time estimate.
services.s1Step2: Structure and design. Content layout first, visual design second. Most corrections happen in this phase, because changing things here is the cheapest it will ever be.
services.s1Step3: Build. Development in the agreed technology, with regular progress reviews so there are no surprises at the end.
services.s1Step4: Handover. Device testing, a speed and SEO check, deployment to the domain, and handover with documentation.
services.s1For1: Small businesses needing a first proper site instead of a social media profile
services.s1For2: Companies with a site a few years old that handles badly on mobile
services.s1For3: Clients who need a landing page with one clear goal, a sign-up or an enquiry
services.s1For4: Projects that call for a custom application rather than bending an off-the-shelf system
services.s1Note1: Content before design. A page arranged around empty boxes always falls apart when the real text arrives.
services.s1Note2: One clear action per page. Five equally prominent buttons means the visitor presses none of them.
services.s1Note3: Speed is not fixed at the end. Decisions about images, fonts and scripts are made during the build, because retrofitting performance always costs more.
services.s1Faq1Q: How long does a website take?
services.s1Faq1A: It depends on the number of pages and on whether it is a presentation site or an application with its own logic. In practice the largest share of the time is not development but gathering content: text, photography and details of the offer. If the content is ready at the start, the timeline shortens more than any technical decision could manage.
services.s1Faq2A: WordPress makes sense when you change content often and want to do it yourself without development work. React makes sense when the site does something specific that off-the-shelf systems handle badly, or when speed and interface behaviour are critical. The decision follows who will maintain the content, not what is currently fashionable.
services.s1Faq3Q: Can I edit the content myself?
services.s1Faq3A: With WordPress yes, and that is usually the main reason for choosing it. With a React build, content is either connected to a dedicated editing system or changed in code. We answer that question before the build starts, because it materially changes both approach and cost.
services.s1Faq4Q: Do you do design too, or do I need it ready?
services.s1Faq4A: I do design as well. If you already have a visual identity, logo and colours, I work inside it. If you do not, the design emerges through the project. Either way I start from the content, because design without content ends up as a nice arrangement of empty frames.
services.s1Faq5Q: What if I already have a domain and hosting?
services.s1Faq5A: Not a problem, I work with what exists. If the hosting is materially slowing the site down I will tell you and explain why, but the decision to move stays yours.
services.s1Faq6A: The best result is when the text comes from you, because you know the business and the customers, and I arrange it into a structure that works on the web. If there is no text, we build it together through a handful of questions. What I will not do is fill a page with empty phrasing so it looks full.
services.s2Title: Websites for holiday rentals, campsites and tourism
services.s2MetaTitle: Websites for tourism and holiday rentals | Martin Bogoje
services.s2MetaDesc: Websites for holiday rentals, campsites and tourism businesses: multilingual, fast-loading galleries and a clear path to a booking enquiry.
services.s2Lead: A guest decides within seconds, and almost always on a phone. The site has to show the property, the surroundings and how to book before their patience runs out.
services.s2Intro1: Tourism content is almost entirely visual, but the decision is made on specifics: how far the sea is, whether there is shade, what the sanitary facilities are like, whether pets are allowed. The site has to reconcile a large amount of practical information with a presentation that stays calm and easy to scan.
services.s2Intro2: So far I have built sites for a campsite, private accommodation, a destination guide and a real estate agency, mostly on the Pelješac peninsula. Every one of those projects followed the same pattern: a lot of photography, an international audience, and visitors arriving on mobile while they are still planning the trip.
services.s2Intro3: A tourism site also has a deadline no other project has: the season. A site published in mid-July has missed the exact window in which guests make their decision, so the build gets planned backwards from the date traffic actually starts.
services.s2Get1: Optimised galleries that load progressively instead of blocking the page
services.s2Get2: A multilingual interface with a separate URL per language, so every version is visible to search engines
services.s2Get3: A clear, always-available route to an enquiry, with no hunting for contact details in the footer
services.s2Get4: A structure that absorbs growth: new units, seasons and amenities are added without a redesign
services.s2Get5: Distances, surroundings and amenities that answer a guest’s questions before they ask them
services.s2Step1: A list of what the guest must learn. Before any design we assemble the questions guests actually ask, because those determine the structure of the site.
services.s2Step2: Photography preparation. Selection, processing and optimisation, because photographs are simultaneously the most important and the most technically demanding part of a tourism site.
services.s2Step3: Build and language versions. Setting up the site and its translations, with a URL structure that tells search engines clearly which version serves which market.
services.s2Step4: Delivery before the season. Testing on phones and slower networks, then publishing with enough time to correct things before traffic starts.
services.s2For1: Private hosts and holiday rentals who want bookings outside the large platforms as well
services.s2For2: Campsites and smaller properties that need to show pitches, amenities and surroundings
services.s2For3: Tourism agencies and destination guides with a larger body of content
services.s2For4: Properties targeting guests from abroad that need the site in several languages
services.s2NoteTitle: What holds tourism sites back most
services.s2Note1: Full-size photographs straight out of the camera. The single most common reason a tourism site takes ten seconds to open.
services.s2Note2: Contact details hidden on a separate page. A guest who has decided should not have to look for how to reach you.
services.s2Note3: Machine translation published unreviewed. A German guest spots a bad German sentence exactly as fast as you spot a bad one in your own language.
services.s2Faq1Q: Do I need a site if I am already on the big platforms?
services.s2Faq1A: Platforms bring guests, but they take a commission and they keep the relationship with the guest. Your own site does not replace the platform; it means the guest who found you there can book directly next time. For that, the site only has to exist, open quickly and show a clear contact.
services.s2Faq2Q: How many languages should the site have?
services.s2Faq2A: As many as the markets your guests actually come from, not as many as sounds impressive. Two well-written versions beat five machine-translated ones. Each language gets its own URL, because a version that exists only as a toggle on the same address effectively does not exist to a search engine.
services.s2Faq3Q: Can I change prices and photos myself each season?
services.s2Faq3A: Yes, and for tourism sites I set it up that way almost every time. Prices, availability and photography change every season, and a solution that needs a developer for each edit stops being updated by its second year.
services.s2Faq4A: It depends what you actually need. For most smaller properties an enquiry form and a clear contact work better than a full booking system, because the guest wants confirmation from the host anyway. If a real system with a calendar and availability is genuinely required, that is a separate project and we treat it as one.
services.s2Faq5Q: When is the best time to build?
services.s2Faq5A: Out of season. You have time to gather photography and text, and the site gets a few months to be indexed before traffic starts. A site published in July misses precisely the period in which guests are deciding.
services.s2Faq6A: It helps more than any technical decision. A tourism site sells an impression, and the impression is carried by the photographs. If professional shots do not exist we work with what there is and pick the best, but it is worth investing in photography before extra functionality.
services.s3Title: Maintenance, speed and technical SEO for an existing site
services.s3MetaTitle: Website maintenance and technical SEO | Martin Bogoje
services.s3MetaDesc: Maintenance for existing websites, faster loading and technical SEO. An audit, fixes ordered by impact, and measurement afterwards.
services.s3Lead: If the site exists but opens slowly, does not show up on Google, or nobody has touched it in two years, what it usually needs is a repair rather than a redesign.
services.s3Intro1: Most sites do not fail because they were built badly. They fail because nobody maintains them. Images get uploaded at full size, plugins go un-updated, text goes stale, and speed degrades until visitors give up before the page opens.
services.s3Intro2: This service starts from measurement rather than assumption. First we establish what is genuinely slowing the site down and what is stopping it from being found, then fix things in order of impact. A redesign only comes into it if the audit shows repair does not make sense.
services.s3Intro3: The audit is worth having even if we then do nothing. You get a list of findings ordered by impact and you can work through it yourself or with somebody else. I would rather tell you the site does not need fixing than charge for work that changes nothing.
services.s3Get1: A speed audit on real devices and networks, with a list of what slows the site most
services.s3Get2: A technical SEO review: titles, meta data, indexing, sitemap and URL structure
services.s3Get3: Image and loading optimisation, usually the single largest speed win available
services.s3Get4: System and plugin updates, with a check that nothing broke afterwards
services.s3Get5: Google Search Console and analytics set up, so you can see what is actually happening
services.s3Step1: Audit. I measure speed, check how the site looks to search engines, and produce a list of findings ordered by impact.
services.s3Step2: Agreeing scope. Together we choose what gets done now and what can wait, because fixing everything at once rarely makes sense.
services.s3Step3: Fixes. Carrying out the agreed changes, verifying that each one genuinely helps and that nothing else broke in the process.
services.s3Step4: Measurement. After the changes we watch the numbers in Search Console and analytics, because the effect of technical SEO only becomes visible over several weeks.
services.s3For1: Sites that load slowly, particularly over mobile networks
services.s3For2: Sites that do not appear on Google even for their own name
services.s3For3: WordPress installations that have gone a long time without updates
services.s3For4: Owners who want to know what is actually happening before investing in a redesign
services.s3NoteTitle: Where the biggest win usually comes from
services.s3Note1: Images. In almost every audit I have run they were the single largest drag on speed.
services.s3Note2: Unnecessary scripts. Plugins and tracking tools loaded on every page but used on one.
services.s3Note3: Missing groundwork. Sites with no sitemap, no Search Console and empty meta descriptions cannot even be measured, let alone fixed.
services.s3Faq1Q: How do I know whether I need a repair or a new site?
services.s3Faq1A: The audit answers that. If the structure is sound and the problem is speed, outdated plugins or missing SEO groundwork, a repair is cheaper and faster. If the site is not responsive, relies on technology that is no longer maintained, or the content is thoroughly out of date, a redesign is the more honest answer.
services.s3Faq2Q: Can you guarantee first place on Google?
services.s3Faq2A: No, and nobody serious can. Nobody controls Google’s algorithm or how strong the competition is for a given term. What can be done is removing the technical obstacles that stop a site from being in the running at all, and then measuring the movement in Search Console.
services.s3Faq3Q: Do you work on sites you did not build?
services.s3Faq3A: Yes, that is actually the most common case. I start by reviewing the state it is in and tell you if something is set up such that repair does not make sense. I will not take on work on a site without that review, because otherwise I would be guessing.
services.s3Faq4A: It can be either. A one-off audit and repair makes sense if the site has been neglected. Ongoing maintenance makes sense if the content is alive and the system and plugins have to be kept current. Which one fits becomes clear after the first audit.
services.s3Faq5A: That is why a backup is taken before updating and why the site itself is checked afterwards, not just the plugin version. If something breaks it goes back to the previous state and we find the cause. The risk of updating is real, but it is smaller than the risk of an un-updated installation.
services.s3Faq6A: Speed shows immediately, the same day. Search visibility does not. Google has to re-crawl the pages and assess the changes, which in practice means several weeks before movement appears in Search Console. Anyone promising faster is promising something they do not control.

pricingPage.metaTitle: How much does a website cost | Pricing | Martin Bogoje
pricingPage.metaDesc: What a website actually costs in Croatia: starting prices, what moves the number up or down, and what is included. No hidden extras.
pricingPage.label: Pricing
pricingPage.title: How much does a website cost
pricingPage.lead: Most sites answer this with "it depends" and leave you without a single figure. Here are the starting prices and, more usefully, what moves them.
pricingPage.intro1: Website prices in Croatia run from a few hundred euros for a simple presentation site to several thousand for systems with their own logic. That range is not a sales tactic; it reflects the fact that very different things get sold under the same name. Adapting a template and designing a site around a specific business are not the same product.
pricingPage.intro2: What follows are starting prices, not quotes. The final figure depends on scope, and scope is only knowable after a short conversation. I would rather tell you the project is smaller than you expected than sell you a package where half the line items serve nobody.
pricingPage.tableNote: Starting prices in euros, excluding VAT. Every project gets a concrete quote once the scope is clear.
pricingPage.landingDesc: One page with one goal: a sign-up, an enquiry, or presenting a single offer.
pricingPage.presentationDesc: Up to about ten pages for a small business, with technical SEO groundwork.
pricingPage.businessDesc: A larger content system, several languages, or a catalogue that keeps growing.
pricingPage.shopDesc: Selling through WooCommerce, including payment and delivery setup.
pricingPage.auditDesc: Speed and technical SEO review of an existing site, with findings ordered by impact.
pricingPage.maintenanceDesc: Updates, backups, small changes and ongoing speed monitoring.
pricingPage.hourlyDesc: For work outside an agreed scope, or occasional adjustments.
pricingPage.factorsIntro: The price almost never depends on how good a site "looks". It depends on these six things:
pricingPage.pagesText: Each page carries design, content and checking. Ten pages is not ten times one, but it is not the same either.
pricingPage.cmsText: If you edit it yourself you need an editing system, and that is additional work. If the content does not change, a static build is cheaper and faster.
pricingPage.contentText: The largest hidden cost. If the text and photography exist at the start, the project flows. If we write them along the way, it takes longer and costs more.
pricingPage.languagesText: Each language means its own URLs, translation and checking. Adding one later costs more than planning for it from the start.
pricingPage.shopText: A shop introduces payments, delivery, tax and stock levels. That is a separate layer of complexity, not an extra page.
pricingPage.integrationsText: Booking systems, CRM, newsletters or external catalogues need connecting and testing, and are usually what pushes a project into a higher bracket.
pricingPage.inc1: Responsive layout, checked on real devices
pricingPage.inc2: Technical SEO groundwork: headings, meta data, sitemap and clean URLs
pricingPage.inc3: Optimised images and a speed check before handover
pricingPage.inc4: Deployment to your domain, with documentation for maintaining it
pricingPage.extra: Domain and hosting are paid to the provider rather than to me, and typically run 10 to 50 euros a year for a domain and 50 to 200 a year for hosting. Professional photography, copy-editing and paid advertising are not included either, though I will tell you when I think they are worth it.
pricingPage.faq1Q: Why is there no fixed price?
pricingPage.faq1A: Because it would be wrong. A five-page presentation site and a catalogue of two hundred products share only a name. Fixed packages usually mean paying for line items you do not need, or being charged extra for the one you do.
pricingPage.faq2Q: Why are your prices lower than an agency’s?
pricingPage.faq2A: Because there is no agency overhead. You work with me directly, with no project manager in between and no margin on somebody else’s work. There is a trade-off: I take on a limited number of projects at once, so the start date depends on what is already running.
pricingPage.faq3A: Usually split in two: part at the start, the rest on delivery. Larger projects are split into phases. All of it is written into the quote before anything begins, so there are no surprises at the end.
pricingPage.faq4Q: What if I need something not on the list?
pricingPage.faq4A: Send a description. If it is feasible you get a quote. If it is not my kind of work, or I think somebody else would do it better, I will tell you that too.
pricingPage.ctaText: A few sentences about the project is enough to estimate scope, timeline and price. You get an answer with no obligation.

blog.indexMetaTitle: Blog on web development and SEO | Martin Bogoje
blog.indexMetaDesc: Writing on website speed, choosing a stack, and sites for tourism. No marketing filler, with concrete examples from real projects.
blog.indexLead: The questions clients actually ask before commissioning a site, answered the way I would answer them in conversation. No tool lists, and no promises of first place on Google.
blog.b1Title: Why your website is slow, and what to do about it
blog.b1MetaTitle: Why your website is slow and how to fix it
blog.b1MetaDesc: The most common reasons a website loads slowly, how to measure the real cause, and what to fix first. No guesswork, no redesign.
blog.b1Lead: A site that takes five seconds to open has lost a share of its visitors before they saw anything. The good news is the cause is almost always the same one, and it is rarely solved by a redesign.
blog.b1Intro: When somebody asks me why their site is slow, they usually already have a theory: the hosting, too many plugins, "something with WordPress". In practice the answer is far more boring nine times out of ten, and better still, far cheaper to fix. Here is what it looks like when you start from measurement instead of guesswork.
blog.b1S1Title: Speed is not an aesthetic question
blog.b1S1A: A waiting visitor has none of the patience you have for your own site. For tourism and service businesses much of the traffic arrives on a phone, often on a mobile network outside town, and there the difference between two and five seconds is the difference between an enquiry and a closed tab.
blog.b1S1B: Google measures this and uses it. Core Web Vitals is a set of metrics describing how quickly the main content appears, how quickly the page responds to a tap, and how much the layout jumps while loading. It is not the dominant ranking factor, but it is the one that decides between two pages of similar quality. If you are in that position, and most small businesses are, speed is one of the few places where an advantage can be won technically.
blog.b1S2Title: Images are almost always the main culprit
blog.b1S2A: In every audit I have run, images were the single largest weight. The reason is simple: a photograph straight out of a camera is several thousand pixels wide and several megabytes, and it gets displayed in a frame a few hundred pixels across. The browser downloads the whole file regardless.
blog.b1S2B: The fix has three parts. First, images are saved in a modern format like WebP, typically two to five times smaller than the same JPEG. Second, several sizes of the same image are prepared so a phone downloads the smaller one. Third, images below the fold load only as the visitor approaches them. Together these often halve the weight of a page with no visible change at all.
blog.b1S3A: The second most common cause is things loading on every page but used on one, or none. A booking calendar that lives on the contact page but whose script loads everywhere. A tracking tool somebody added three years ago that nobody looks at. A gallery installed to try out, then left in place.
blog.b1S3B: On WordPress this accumulates invisibly, because each plugin brings its own CSS and JavaScript. It is not unusual for a site to load ten stylesheets and twenty scripts, a third of which are actually used. Removing inactive plugins and limiting the rest to the pages that need them is usually the second largest win, right behind images.
blog.b1S4Title: Hosting and where the server sits
blog.b1S4A: Hosting is the real cause less often than people assume, but when it is, you can see it immediately: the page does nothing for a long time, then loads normally. That waiting period is time to first byte, and it depends on the server rather than on your site.
blog.b1S4B: For Croatian visitors it also matters where the server physically is. The cheapest plans tend to sit on shared hardware with several hundred other sites, and then your speed depends on what the neighbours are doing. Moving to decent European hosting usually costs less per month than an hour of development work, which makes it one of the few decisions where the answer is almost always obvious.
blog.b1S5A: Before any fix, it is worth measuring. PageSpeed Insights is free and gives two things: a lab test and, if the site has enough traffic, real data from actual visitors. That real-world data is what Google uses, so it matters more than the score in the test.
blog.b1S5B: Search Console shows the same picture over time and grouped by page type, which is more useful than a single test. If the numbers do not move in the right direction within a few weeks of a fix, the wrong thing was fixed. That is the only reliable way to avoid an expensive redesign that solves a problem which was never there.
blog.b1L1: Open the site on a phone using mobile data rather than wi-fi, and time the wait
blog.b1L2: Check the weight of the largest image on the homepage; anything over 300 KB is a candidate
blog.b1L3: Look at the list of active plugins and ask whether each one is genuinely used
blog.b1L4: Run PageSpeed Insights and read the field data, not just the score
blog.b1L5: Turn on Search Console if it is not already, because without it there is no history
blog.b1CloseTitle: When a fix is not enough
blog.b1Close: A repair makes sense when the structure is sound and the problem is speed, neglected plugins or missing technical groundwork. If the site is not responsive, runs on a system that is no longer maintained, or the content is so out of date it needs rewriting anyway, then a new site is the more honest answer. An audit shows which of the two you are looking at within a few hours, and it is worth doing before committing to the more expensive option.
blog.b2Title: WordPress or React: how to choose for your site
blog.b2MetaTitle: WordPress or React: what to choose for a website
blog.b2MetaDesc: Comparing WordPress and React for small businesses: when each makes sense, what they cost over time, and the question that actually decides it.
blog.b2Lead: This is a question developers enjoy and clients rarely benefit from. The decision almost never turns on which technology is better, but on who will maintain the content.
blog.b2Intro: If you have been looking for someone to build your site, you have probably had contradictory advice. One says WordPress because it is simple, another says WordPress is slow and offers something modern. Both can be right, because they are answering different questions. Here is how I make the call, and which question actually settles it.
blog.b2S1Title: The question is not which technology is better
blog.b2S1A: Both WordPress and React can produce a fast, tidy, well-ranked site, and both can produce a slow, unmaintainable one. The technology sets an upper bound; the execution determines the result. I have seen WordPress sites that load in a second and React applications that barely function on a phone.
blog.b2S1B: So the first question is never technical. I ask who will change the content, how often, and how much that person is willing to learn. The answer usually resolves ninety percent of the dilemma before any tool gets mentioned.
blog.b2S2A: WordPress is the answer when the content is alive. If you change prices by season, add properties, publish news, or want to swap photographs yourself without emailing a developer, you need an editing system, and WordPress is the most widespread one in Croatia. That also means it is easier to find somebody who knows it if our paths diverge.
blog.b2S2B: The price of that flexibility is maintenance. WordPress and its plugins need regular updates, and every plugin is something that can break or slow the site down. That is not a reason to avoid it, but it is a line item to plan for: an installation nobody has updated in two years is a security problem, not just technical debt.
blog.b2S3A: React makes sense when the site does something specific that off-the-shelf systems handle badly, or when speed and interface behaviour are part of the product. Calculators, configurators, interactive displays, applications with their own logic. It also makes sense when the content barely changes, because then there is no reason to pay for and maintain an entire CMS layer.
blog.b2S3B: What often goes unsaid is that a React site is not automatically good for search engines without extra work. If content is drawn only in the browser, some of the tools that read the page will see nothing. There is a solution, called prerendering or server-side rendering, but it is work somebody has to do. If you are offered a React site, ask how that part is handled.
blog.b2S4A: The most expensive mistake is choosing the technology before knowing who maintains the content. That is where React sites come from whose owner cannot change a phone number without an invoice, and WordPress installs with fifteen plugins on a site that has not changed since launch.
blog.b2S4B: The second common mistake is choosing by novelty. Technology that was popular five years ago is often a burden today, and what is popular now will be in the same position in five years. A more useful question than "is this modern" is "will somebody be able to take this over in three years".
blog.b2S5Title: Cost over time, not just at the start
blog.b2S5A: The initial price is the visible part. What gets calculated less often is the cost across several years: hosting, updates, small changes, and the time you spend maintaining it yourself. WordPress usually has a lower entry price and higher maintenance. A static or React build usually has the opposite profile.
blog.b2S5B: So I ask how long the site needs to last. For a site that is an advertisement for one season and a site that underpins the business for the next five years, the answer is not the same, even when they look almost identical.
blog.b2ListTitle: Five questions that decide it for you
blog.b2L1: Who will change the content, and how often
blog.b2L2: Does the site do anything beyond displaying information
blog.b2L3: How much are you willing to spend on maintenance each year
blog.b2L4: Does the site need to exist in several languages
blog.b2L5: How long do you expect this version of the site to last
blog.b2Close: If you change the content yourself and often, take WordPress and budget for maintenance. If the content rarely changes or the site does something specific, a static or React build gives you a faster and quieter result. If you are not sure, that is a sign the conversation needs to be about content first, not technology.
blog.b3Title: Websites for holiday rentals and campsites: what guests look for
blog.b3MetaTitle: Websites for holiday rentals: what guests look for
blog.b3MetaDesc: What a tourism website needs before a guest sends an enquiry: photography, practical detail, languages and speed. From projects on Pelješac.
blog.b3Lead: A guest is looking at your site on a phone, often with five other tabs open. The decision happens within seconds, and almost never on the basis of what you think matters most.
blog.b3Intro: I have built sites for a campsite, private accommodation and a destination guide, mostly on the Pelješac peninsula. The pattern repeats every time: a lot of photography, an audience from abroad, and visitors who are still planning the trip. This is what those projects showed actually affects whether an enquiry arrives.
blog.b3S1A: A guest does not read, they scan. The first screen has to deliver three things: what the property is, where it is, and what the surroundings look like. If they have to scroll to work out whether they are looking at an apartment or a campsite, you have already lost them to the next open tab.
blog.b3S1B: That makes the opening photograph the hardest-working element on the entire site. An aerial shot of the bay or a view from the terrace says more than three paragraphs of text, and it is one of the few places where paying for professional photography beats paying for extra functionality.
blog.b3S2Title: Photography is both the most important and the most demanding part
blog.b3S2A: A tourism site sells an impression, and the impression is carried by photographs. At the same time, photographs are the main reason tourism sites take ten seconds to open. A gallery of thirty images straight from a camera is tens of megabytes, which is unusable on a mobile network in July.
blog.b3S2B: The answer is not fewer photographs but smarter delivery. Images get prepared in several sizes, saved in a modern format, and loaded progressively as the guest scrolls. The gallery stays rich and the page opens immediately. This is a difference a guest will never notice but will absolutely feel.
blog.b3S3Title: The practical details guests want and rarely get
blog.b3S3A: After the impression come the specifics, and this is where most sites fall down. How far the sea is, in walking minutes rather than as the crow flies. Whether there is shade. What the sanitary facilities are like. Whether there is parking. Whether pets are allowed. Whether the air conditioning works. How long the drive from the ferry takes.
blog.b3S3B: Every one of those questions the site fails to answer becomes an email you have to write, or a guest who gave up rather than ask. The list of questions you actually receive in enquiries is the best possible blueprint for the structure of the site, and it is worth compiling before any design starts.
blog.b3S4Title: Languages by market, not by ambition
blog.b3S4A: Guests come from specific countries and you already know which from your own bookings. If those are Germany, Poland and Austria, then German and Polish make sense, and Italian does not simply because it sounds good. Two well-written versions always beat five machine-translated ones, because a guest spots a bad sentence in their own language as fast as you would.
blog.b3S4B: Technically, it matters that each language has its own URL. A version that exists only as a toggle on the same address effectively does not exist to a search engine, so a German guest searching in German will never reach it. This is one of the few technical decisions that directly affects the number of enquiries.
blog.b3S5Title: Platforms are not a substitute for your own site
blog.b3S5A: The large platforms bring guests and that is real value. But they take a commission, they own the relationship with the guest, and they can change the rules whenever they like. Your own site does not replace the platform; it means the guest who found you there can book directly next time.
blog.b3S5B: That does not require a booking system. For most smaller properties an enquiry form and a clearly visible contact work better, because the guest wants confirmation from the host before paying anyway. A full system with a calendar and availability only makes sense once the number of units or the volume of enquiries justifies it.
blog.b3L1: An opening photograph that explains in one second where you are and what the property is
blog.b3L2: Answers to practical questions, including distance to the sea in walking minutes
blog.b3L3: Contact details visible from every page, not only on a separate contact page
blog.b3L4: Language versions on their own URLs, for the markets guests actually come from
blog.b3L5: Galleries that load progressively, so the page opens on a mobile network too
blog.b3CloseTitle: The season is a deadline nobody moves
blog.b3Close: A tourism site has one deadline no other project has. A site published in mid-July has missed the window in which guests decide, and search engines need several weeks before they even begin showing it. So the build gets planned backwards from the date traffic actually starts, and the best time to do the work is winter, when there is room to gather photography and text.
